claim: Acute restraint stress leads to a marked increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the lateral septum compared to controls.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Kubo et al., 2002), acute restraint stress led to a marked increase in the number of c-fos+ cells in the LS compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Unpaired Student's t-test, *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased c-fos+ cells in the LS after restraint stress, with statistical significance (p<0.05), and is also supported by citation to previous work (Kubo et al., 2002).

claim: The lateral septum is part of the anterior limbic system and regulates several emotional behaviors, particularly stress, anxiety, and aggression.
source: The LS is part of the anterior limbic system and is known to regulate several emotional behaviors, particularly stress, anxiety, and aggression (Kubo et al., 2002; Anthony et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Kubo et al., 2002; Anthony et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2016) that establish the role of the LS in emotional behaviors.

claim: Optogenetic activation of neurons in the lateral septum has a negative effect on feeding.
source: In addition, a previous study from our group and another have shown that optogenetic activation of neurons in the LS has a negative effect on feeding (Azevedo et al., 2019; Sweeney and Yang, 2016), raising the possibility that specific neurons in this region might link restraint stress to a non-homeostatic reduction in food intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Azevedo et al., 2019; Sweeney and Yang, 2016) that demonstrated the effect of LS neuron activation on feeding.

claim: PhosphoTrap is an unbiased transcriptomic method to molecularly profile activated neurons.
source: Next, we set out to determine the molecular identity of the neurons in the LS that are activated by acute restraint stress using PhosphoTrap, an unbiased transcriptomic method to molecularly profile activated neurons (Knight et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knight et al., 2012, which describes the PhosphoTrap method.

claim: Neuronal activation results in a cascade of signaling events culminating in the phosphorylation of the ribosomal protein S6 (pS6).
source: This method takes advantage of the fact that neuronal activation results in a cascade of signaling events culminating in the phosphorylation of the ribosomal protein S6 (pS6).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about neuronal signaling cascades and is referenced in the context of the PhosphoTrap method.

claim: Neurotensin (Nts) gene expression was enriched 2.41-fold in the lateral septum samples from mice exposed to acute restraint stress compared to control mice.
source: We found enrichment for several markers, including the gene for the neuropeptide neurotensin (Nts, a 2.41-fold increase compared to control samples; Schroeder et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PhosphoTrap RNA sequencing showing 2.41-fold enrichment of Nts, and is also supported by citation to Schroeder et al., 2019.

claim: Neurotensin mRNA was enriched 3.6-fold in the lateral septum samples from mice exposed to acute restraint stress compared to control mice as confirmed by qPCR.
source: We confirmed the enrichment using qPCR and found a 3.6-fold enrichment in neurotensin mRNA in the samples from the lateral septum of mice exposed to acute restraint stress compared to samples from control mice (Figure 1C, Unpaired Student's t-test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental qPCR data showing 3.6-fold enrichment with statistical significance (p<0.05).

claim: Approximately 37 cells co-expressing Fos and Nts were found in the lateral septum of stressed mice compared to 22 cells in non-stressed control mice.
source: We found significant colocalization of Fos and Nts in the LS after mice were subjected to restraint stress compared to controls (~37 cells in stressed mice vs. 22 cells in non-stressed control mice; Unpaired Student's t-test, p<0.05, Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing colocalization of Fos and Nts with statistical significance (p<0.05).

claim: The increased colocalization between Fos and Nts in stressed mice was due to both an increase in the levels of Fos in Nts neurons and a concomitant induction of Nts mRNA during stress.
source: We also found that the increased colocalization between Fos and Nts in stressed mice was due to both an increase in the levels of Fos in Nts neurons and a concomitant induction of Nts mRNA during stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The activity of Nts neurons as well as the expression of the Nts gene in the lateral septum is regulated by acute restraint stress.
source: These results suggest that the activity of Nts neurons as well as the expression of the Nts gene in the LS is regulated by acute restraint stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased Fos and Nts colocalization and increased Nts mRNA levels during stress.

claim: Acute restraint stress for 1 hour significantly decreased food consumption for 2 hours after the stress in mice.
source: We thus assayed food intake after 1 hr of acute restraint stress and observed a highly significant decrease in consumption for the ensuing 2 hrs (Figure 2A, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, *p<0.05, ***p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased food intake after restraint stress with statistical significance (p<0.05, p<0.001), as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Injection of CNO into Nts-cre mice expressing excitatory DREADD increased c-fos expression in the lateral septum.
source: As expected, injection of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) into these mice increased c-fos expression in the LS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Unpaired Student's t-test, p<0.01)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased c-fos expression after CNO injection with statistical significance (p<0.01), as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons significantly decreased food intake compared to control mice.
source: As expected, injection of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) into these mice increased c-fos expression in the LS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Unpaired Student's t-test, p<0.01) and significantly decreased food intake compared to mice treated with CNO after injection of a control Cre-dependent mCherry AAV into Nts-cre mice (Figure 2B, red bars vs. black bars, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, ***p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased food intake after chemogenetic activation with statistical significance (p<0.001), as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The decrease in food intake after LSNts neuron activation was evident after 1 hour and persisted for 4, 8, and 24 hours after a single CNO injection.
source: This robust decrease in food intake was evident after 1 hr and persisted for 4, 8, and 24 hr after a single CNO injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing sustained decrease in food intake over multiple time points, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Chronic stimulation of Nts neurons in the lateral septum for 3 days significantly decreased food intake.
source: Chronic stimulation of Nts neurons for 3 d in the LS also significantly decreased food intake (Figure 2C, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, **p<0.01, ****p<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased food intake after chronic stimulation with statistical significance (p<0.01, p<0.0001), as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chronic stimulation of Nts neurons in the lateral septum for 3 days significantly reduced body weight.
source: Chronic stimulation of Nts neurons for 3 d in the LS also significantly decreased food intake (Figure 2C, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, **p<0.01, ****p<0.0001) and significantly reduced body weight relative to the aforementioned controls (Figure 2D, Unpaired Student's t-test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced body weight after chronic stimulation with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fasted mice exposed to acute restraint stress for 1 hour consumed significantly less food during refeeding than control mice.
source: We found that fasted mice that had also been exposed to acute restraint stress for 1 hr consumed significantly less food during refeeding than controls (Figure 2E, Unpaired Student's t-test, *p<0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased food intake during refeeding after stress with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Acute stress can override the hyperphagia that follows an overnight fast.
source: We found that fasted mice that had also been exposed to acute restraint stress for 1 hr consumed significantly less food during refeeding than controls (Figure 2E, Unpaired Student's t-test, *p<0.05), indicating that acute stress can override the hyperphagia that follows an overnight fast.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that stressed fasted mice ate less than control fasted mice during refeeding.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons in mice suppressed food intake in mice that were refed after an overnight fast.
source: Consistent with this, chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons in mice also suppressed food intake in mice that were refed after that an overnight fast (Figure 2F, Unpaired Student's t-test, *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing suppressed food intake after chemogenetic activation in fasted mice with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Acute inhibition of LSNts neurons led to an increase in food intake after CNO injection compared to mCherry controls in the first 2 hours.
source: Acute inhibition of LSNts neurons led to an increase in food intake after CNO injection compared to mCherry controls in the first 2 hr (Figure 2G, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, ***p<0.001) and at 8 and 24 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased food intake after inhibition of LSNts neurons with statistical significance (p<0.001), as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Chronic inhibition of Nts neurons in the lateral septum for 3 days produced an increase in food intake that was significant on the 3rd day.
source: Chronic inhibition of Nts neurons in the LS for 3 d produced an increase in food intake that was significant on the 3rd day (Figure 2H, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, *p<0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased food intake on day 3 after chronic inhibition with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Chronic inhibition of Nts neurons in the lateral septum for 3 days did not increase body weight.
source: Chronic inhibition of Nts neurons in the LS for 3 d produced an increase in food intake that was significant on the 3rd day (Figure 2H, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, *p<0.05) but did not increase body weight (Figure 2I, Unpaired Student's t-test, p=0.83).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant change in body weight (p=0.83), as shown in Figure 2I.

claim: LSNts neurons negatively regulate food intake in mice.
source: These results show that LSNts neurons negatively regulate food intake in mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that activation of LSNts neurons decreases food intake and inhibition increases food intake.

claim: LSNts chemogenetic activation did not alter open field thigmotaxis, general locomotion, neophobia, anxiety-related behaviors in elevated plus maze, or novelty-suppressed feeding.
source: Interestingly, LSNts chemogenetic activation did not alter other behaviors often associated with stressful conditions. This was evaluated by assaying open field thigmotaxis, general locomotion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C), neophobia or anxiety-related behaviors when animals were in an open-field with novelty (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), in an elevated plus maze (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–G), or during novelty-suppressed feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H). Activation of LSNts neurons failed to elicit an effect on any of these other behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from multiple behavioral assays showing no significant effects, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-H.

claim: LSNts neurons are activated by restraint stress and reduce food intake, but do not play a discernible role in anxiogenic behaviors.
source: In aggregate, these data show LSNts neurons are activated by restraint stress and reduce food intake, but do not play a discernible role in anxiogenic behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing LSNts activation by stress, effects on feeding, and lack of effects on anxiety behaviors.

claim: The majority of neurons in the lateral septum are GABAergic.
source: The majority of the neurons in the LS are GABAergic and a number of neuropeptides and specific receptors are expressed in this region in addition to neurotensin (Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lein et al., 2007, which describes the neuronal composition of the lateral septum.

claim: A number of neuropeptides and specific receptors are expressed in the lateral septum in addition to neurotensin.
source: The majority of the neurons in the LS are GABAergic and a number of neuropeptides and specific receptors are expressed in this region in addition to neurotensin (Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lein et al., 2007, which describes the molecular diversity of the lateral septum.

claim: Several genes were significantly enriched in LSNts neurons including Gfp, Nts, Sst, Glp1r, Cartpt, and Mc3r.
source: Several genes were significantly enriched in the immunoprecipitated fraction (IP) including Gfp, Nts, Sst, Glp1r, Cartpt, and Mc3r (Figure 3B and C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from viral-TRAP RNA sequencing showing enrichment of these genes, as shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Approximately 80% of septal Nts neurons co-express Slc32a1 (Vgat), a marker of GABAergic neurons.
source: We confirmed the expression of these transcripts using qPCR of the precipitated RNAs (Figure 3C) and in situ hybridization which also showed that ~80% of septal Nts neurons co-express Slc32a1 (Vgat), a marker of GABAergic neurons (Figure 3D, Unpaired Student's t-test, **p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing colocalization with statistical significance (p<0.01), as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 70% of LSNts neurons express Glp1r.
source: We also verified the co-expression of Nts with Glp1r, Sst, Cartpt, and Mc3r using in situ hybridization, and confirmed that 70% of LSNts neurons express Glp1r, 50% express Sst, 40% express Cartpt, and 20% express Mc3r (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing colocalization percentages, as shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: 50% of LSNts neurons express Sst.
source: We also verified the co-expression of Nts with Glp1r, Sst, Cartpt, and Mc3r using in situ hybridization, and confirmed that 70% of LSNts neurons express Glp1r, 50% express Sst, 40% express Cartpt, and 20% express Mc3r (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing colocalization percentages, as shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: 40% of LSNts neurons express Cartpt.
source: We also verified the co-expression of Nts with Glp1r, Sst, Cartpt, and Mc3r using in situ hybridization, and confirmed that 70% of LSNts neurons express Glp1r, 50% express Sst, 40% express Cartpt, and 20% express Mc3r (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing colocalization percentages, as shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: 20% of LSNts neurons express Mc3r.
source: We also verified the co-expression of Nts with Glp1r, Sst, Cartpt, and Mc3r using in situ hybridization, and confirmed that 70% of LSNts neurons express Glp1r, 50% express Sst, 40% express Cartpt, and 20% express Mc3r (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing colocalization percentages, as shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: Cartpt is known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas.
source: Many of the genes co-expressed with Nts in LSNts neurons are known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas, including Cartpt (Kristensen et al., 1998), Glp1r (Kanoski et al., 2016), Mc3r (Marks et al., 2006), and Sst (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kristensen et al., 1998, which describes the role of Cartpt in feeding behavior.

claim: Glp1r is known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas.
source: Many of the genes co-expressed with Nts in LSNts neurons are known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas, including Cartpt (Kristensen et al., 1998), Glp1r (Kanoski et al., 2016), Mc3r (Marks et al., 2006), and Sst (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kanoski et al., 2016, which describes the role of Glp1r in feeding behavior.

claim: Mc3r is known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas.
source: Many of the genes co-expressed with Nts in LSNts neurons are known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas, including Cartpt (Kristensen et al., 1998), Glp1r (Kanoski et al., 2016), Mc3r (Marks et al., 2006), and Sst (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Marks et al., 2006, which describes the role of Mc3r in feeding behavior.

claim: Sst is known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas.
source: Many of the genes co-expressed with Nts in LSNts neurons are known to regulate feeding behavior via effects on other brain areas, including Cartpt (Kristensen et al., 1998), Glp1r (Kanoski et al., 2016), Mc3r (Marks et al., 2006), and Sst (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2018, which describes the role of Sst in feeding behavior.

claim: Activation of Glp1r neurons within the lateral septum with the Glp1r agonist exendin-4 resulted in a robust decrease in food intake after 2, 12, and 24 hours.
source: Similar to chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons, activation of Glp1r neurons within the LS with the Glp1r agonist exendin-4 (Figure 3J and K) resulted in a robust decrease in food intake after 2, 12, and 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased food intake after exendin-4 treatment, as shown in Figure 3J, K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of Glp1r neurons in the lateral septum reduced food intake.
source: In addition, chemogenetic activation of Glp1r neurons by injecting the activatory hM3Dq DREADD into the LS of Glp1r-cre mice also reduced food intake (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, *p<0.05, ****p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased food intake after chemogenetic activation with statistical significance (p<0.05, p<0.0001).

claim: Food intake was unchanged after infusion of the Mc3r agonist (gamma-melanocyte-stimulating hormone; y-msh) into the septum.
source: By contrast, food intake was unchanged after infusion of the Mc3r agonist (gamma-melanocyte-stimulating hormone; y-msh) into the septum or activation of Cartpt or Sst neurons by injecting an activatory DREADD (hM3Dq) into Cartpt-cre and Sst-cre animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in food intake after y-msh infusion, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Food intake was unchanged after activation of Cartpt neurons by injecting an activatory DREADD into Cartpt-cre animals.
source: By contrast, food intake was unchanged after infusion of the Mc3r agonist (gamma-melanocyte-stimulating hormone; y-msh) into the septum or activation of Cartpt or Sst neurons by injecting an activatory DREADD (hM3Dq) into Cartpt-cre and Sst-cre animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in food intake after Cartpt neuron activation, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Food intake was unchanged after activation of Sst neurons by injecting an activatory DREADD into Sst-cre animals.
source: By contrast, food intake was unchanged after infusion of the Mc3r agonist (gamma-melanocyte-stimulating hormone; y-msh) into the septum or activation of Cartpt or Sst neurons by injecting an activatory DREADD (hM3Dq) into Cartpt-cre and Sst-cre animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in food intake after Sst neuron activation, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Activation of Cartpt, Glp1r, and Sst subpopulations in the lateral septum had no effect on arm exploration in an elevated plus maze.
source: Activation of these other LSNts subpopulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I) also had no effect on arm exploration as assessed using an elevated plus maze (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J–L), suggesting that they do not elicit anxiety.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from elevated plus maze tests showing no effects on anxiety-related behavior, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J-L.

claim: Glp-1 signaling has been shown to exert an anorectic effect.
source: Glp-1 signaling has been shown to exert an anorectic effect and blocking of Glp1r signaling using specific antagonists has been shown to blunt stress-induced anorexia (Terrill et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Terrill et al., 2018, which describes the anorectic effects of Glp-1 signaling.

claim: Blocking of Glp1r signaling using specific antagonists has been shown to blunt stress-induced anorexia.
source: Glp-1 signaling has been shown to exert an anorectic effect and blocking of Glp1r signaling using specific antagonists has been shown to blunt stress-induced anorexia (Terrill et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Terrill et al., 2018, which describes the effects of blocking Glp1r signaling on stress-induced anorexia.

claim: After acute restraint stress, Fos expression was significantly increased only in LSNts neurons that also co-express Glp1r.
source: After acute restraint stress, we observed significantly increased expression of Fos only in LSNts neurons that also co-express Glp1r, while Fos expression was unchanged in Glp1r neurons that do not express Nts (Figure 3M, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, *p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing increased Fos expression in Nts/Glp1r neurons with statistical significance (p<0.01), as shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Infusion of Exendin-4 (ex4), a Glp1r agonist, into the lateral septum increased Fos expression in approximately 65% of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r.
source: Furthermore, infusion of Exendin-4 (ex4), a Glp1r agonist, into the LS increased Fos expression in ~65% of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r (Figure 3N, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, ****p<0.0001), but not in Nts neurons that do not co-express Glp1r (Figure 3N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing increased Fos expression after exendin-4 treatment with statistical significance (p<0.0001), as shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Exendin-4 infusion into the lateral septum did not increase Fos expression in Nts neurons that do not co-express Glp1r.
source: Furthermore, infusion of Exendin-4 (ex4), a Glp1r agonist, into the LS increased Fos expression in ~65% of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r (Figure 3N, Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc, ****p<0.0001), but not in Nts neurons that do not co-express Glp1r (Figure 3N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization showing no change in Fos expression in Nts neurons without Glp1r, as shown in Figure 3N.

claim: There is heterogeneity of the Nts population in the lateral septum.
source: These results demonstrate the heterogeneity of the Nts population in the LS and identify a stress-responsive subpopulation of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r that negatively regulates food intake and further shows that Glp-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) signaling to this subpopulation of LSNts neurons regulates their activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential expression of multiple markers (Glp1r, Sst, Cartpt, Mc3r) in LSNts neurons and differential responses to stress and Glp1r agonists.

claim: A stress-responsive subpopulation of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r negatively regulates food intake.
source: These results demonstrate the heterogeneity of the Nts population in the LS and identify a stress-responsive subpopulation of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r that negatively regulates food intake and further shows that Glp-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) signaling to this subpopulation of LSNts neurons regulates their activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r are activated by stress and that Glp1r activation reduces food intake.

claim: Glp-1 signaling to the subpopulation of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r regulates their activity.
source: These results demonstrate the heterogeneity of the Nts population in the LS and identify a stress-responsive subpopulation of LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r that negatively regulates food intake and further shows that Glp-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) signaling to this subpopulation of LSNts neurons regulates their activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that exendin-4 (a Glp1r agonist) increases Fos expression in LSNts neurons co-expressing Glp1r.

claim: LSNts neurons have dense axonal projections in the lateral hypothalamus.
source: We found dense axonal projections of these neurons in the hypothalamus, in particular the lateral hypothalamus (LH, Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from viral tracing showing dense projections to the LH, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The lateral hypothalamus is a well-established brain region regulating food intake.
source: The LH is a well-established brain region regulating food intake (Morrison et al., 1958)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Morrison et al., 1958, which describes the role of the LH in food intake regulation.

claim: Optogenetic activation of LSNts terminals in the lateral hypothalamus with blue light led to a significant increase in c-fos expression in LSNts neurons (approximately 181 c-fos+ neurons for Chr2 vs. approximately 8.5 for mCherry).
source: Optogenetic activation of this pathway with blue light led to a significant increase in c-fos expression in the LSNts neurons (~181 c-fos+ neurons for Chr2 vs. ~8.5 for mCherry) and a subset of neurons in the LH (~128 c-fos+ neurons for Chr2 vs. ~35 for mCherry, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D, Unpaired Student's t-test, **p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry showing increased c-fos expression with statistical significance (p<0.01), as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of LSNts terminals in the lateral hypothalamus with blue light led to a significant increase in c-fos expression in a subset of neurons in the lateral hypothalamus (approximately 128 c-fos+ neurons for Chr2 vs. approximately 35 for mCherry).
source: Optogenetic activation of this pathway with blue light led to a significant increase in c-fos expression in the LSNts neurons (~181 c-fos+ neurons for Chr2 vs. ~8.5 for mCherry) and a subset of neurons in the LH (~128 c-fos+ neurons for Chr2 vs. ~35 for mCherry, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D, Unpaired Student's t-test, **p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry showing increased c-fos expression with statistical significance (p<0.01), as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Optogenetic activation of LSNts terminals in the lateral hypothalamus led to a reversible and significant decrease of food intake in mice expressing ChR2 compared to controls expressing mCherry.
source: We then used a 1 hr OFF-ON-OFF protocol to evaluate food intake before, during, and after light stimulation of LSNts terminals in the LH and observed a reversible and significant decrease of food intake in mice expressing ChR2 compared to controls expressing mCherry (Figure 4C, Two-way ANOVA with post-hoc Bonferroni correction, *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic feeding experiments showing decreased food intake with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Activation of LH-projecting LSNts neurons led to approximately 50% decrease in food intake compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, similar to the effect of activating the entire LSNTS population of neurons, activation of the LH-projecting LSNts neurons led to a ~50% decrease in food intake compared to controls (Figure 4C, right panel, Unpaired Student's t-test, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic feeding experiments showing approximately 50% decrease in food intake with statistical significance (p<0.01), as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Activation of LH-projecting LSNts neurons had no effect on locomotion or anxiety as assessed by open field or elevated plus maze tests.
source: We also evaluated whether the activation of LH-projecting LSNts neurons had any effect on locomotion or anxiety and found no differences during open field or elevated plus maze tests (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays showing no significant effects, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: LSNts neurons did not increase their calcium signal when animals were rendered completely immobile during manual restraint.
source: Surprisingly, we did not see a change in the calcium signal when the animal was rendered completely immobile. Rather, we only found increases in the calcium signal when animals were actively struggling to escape immediately either before or after the manual restraint.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings during manual immobilization.

claim: LSNts neurons showed increases in calcium signal when animals were actively struggling to escape immediately before or after manual restraint.
source: Surprisingly, we did not see a change in the calcium signal when the animal was rendered completely immobile. Rather, we only found increases in the calcium signal when animals were actively struggling to escape immediately either before or after the manual restraint. The reduced activity LSNts neurons was seen both when the animals were completely immobilized or when they had ceased struggling (Figure 5A, One-way ANOVA, multiple comparisons with Bonferroni post-hoc, *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings showing increased calcium signals during struggling with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LSNts neurons were significantly activated while animals were suspended by their tails and actively struggled.
source: We then recorded LSNts calcium signals in animals that were subjected to 1 min of being suspended by their tails during which time the animals struggle and actively try to escape. Consistent with the previous results, we observed significant activation of LSNts neurons while the animals were suspended and actively struggled (Figure 5B, Paired Student's t-test, *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings during tail suspension showing increased calcium signals with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Movement of a robotic spider toward mice induced a rapid retreat and led mice to immediately return to the inside of an acrylic nest.
source: We observed that the forward movement of the robotic spider toward the mouse induced a rapid retreat and led the mice to immediately return to the inside the acrylic nest (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the robotic spider predator paradigm, as shown in Video 1.

claim: Movement of the robotic spider toward mice led to strong activation of LSNts neurons that persisted until the mouse had returned to the nest.
source: We simultaneously used in vivo fiber photometry to monitor the activity of LSNts neurons during this simulated predator attack and found that movement of the robotic spider toward the mouse led to strong activation of LSNts neurons that persisted until the mouse had returned to the nest (Figure 5C, Paired Student's t-test, *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings during robotic spider attack showing increased calcium signals with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A rapid and sustained increase in LSNts calcium signal was observed when the nest was removed and mice were exposed to the robotic spider.
source: Similarly, we observed a rapid and sustained increase in the calcium signal when the nest was removed and mice were exposed to the robotic spider (Figure 5D, Paired Student's t-test, *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings during nest removal showing increased calcium signals with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LSNts neurons are activated by stressful stimuli in which the animal's response includes active movement such as struggling or flight (active coping strategies).
source: In aggregate, these results show that LSNts neurons are activated by stressful stimuli in which the animal's response includes active movement such as struggling or flight (active coping strategies) and further suggest that these neurons are not activated by stressful stimuli associated with immobility or freezing, that is, passive coping responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing LSNts activation during tail suspension, robotic spider attack, and foot shock, but not during immobilization or freezing.

claim: LSNts neurons are not activated by stressful stimuli associated with immobility or freezing (passive coping responses).
source: In aggregate, these results show that LSNts neurons are activated by stressful stimuli in which the animal's response includes active movement such as struggling or flight (active coping strategies) and further suggest that these neurons are not activated by stressful stimuli associated with immobility or freezing, that is, passive coping responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no LSNts activation during immobilization or freezing behavior.

claim: During contextual fear conditioning training, LSNts calcium signals were increased following the foot shock, time-locked with movement as mice jumped away from the shock.
source: Consistent with the prior results, we found that during the training session, LSNts calcium signals were increased following the foot shock, time-locked with movement as the mice jumped away from the shock (Figure 5E and F, Paired Student's t-test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings during fear conditioning training showing increased calcium signals with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: During contextual fear conditioning recall test, when mice exhibited freezing behavior, the LSNts calcium signal was significantly decreased compared to the period before the onset of freezing.
source: However, during the recall test the following day, when mice exhibited freezing behavior after being placed in the chamber that they associated with a foot shock, the LSNts calcium signal was significantly decreased compared to the period before the onset of freezing (Figure 5G, Paired Student's t-test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings during fear conditioning recall showing decreased calcium signals with statistical significance (p<0.05), as shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The activity of LSNts neurons is tuned to active, but not passive, responses to stressful stimuli.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with the possibility that the activity of these neurons is tuned to active, but not passive, responses to stressful stimuli.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential LSNts activation during active versus passive coping behaviors.

claim: LSNts neurons remain active until the animal is in an environment that is either perceived to be 'safe' or until the animal freezes as part of a passive coping strategy.
source: They also indicate that these neurons remain active until the animal is in an environment that is either perceived to be 'safe' or until the animal freezes as part of a passive coping strategy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing sustained LSNts activity during escape until reaching the nest and decreased activity during freezing.

claim: No significant temporal correlation was found between calcium signals in LSNts neurons and feeding.
source: By contrast, we did not find any significant temporal correlation between calcium signals in LSNts neurons and feeding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D) or voluntary movement in an open field arena in the absence of danger signals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings showing no correlation with feeding, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: No significant temporal correlation was found between calcium signals in LSNts neurons and voluntary movement in an open field arena in the absence of danger signals.
source: By contrast, we did not find any significant temporal correlation between calcium signals in LSNts neurons and feeding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D) or voluntary movement in an open field arena in the absence of danger signals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium recordings showing no correlation with voluntary movement, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Stress elicits a pleiotropic set of adaptive physiologic and behavioral responses enabling animals to rapidly respond to threatening situations.
source: Stress elicits a pleiotropic set of adaptive physiologic and behavioral responses enabling animals to rapidly respond to threatening situations.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about stress responses.

claim: Stress responses include suppression of other behaviors such as feeding while animals initiate defensive behaviors.
source: These responses include suppression of other behaviors such as feeding while animals initiate defensive behaviors.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about stress-induced behavioral changes.

claim: The inhibition of consummatory behaviors when animals are threatened decreases an animal's vulnerability to predation.
source: Accordingly, the inhibition of consummatory behaviors when animals are threatened decreases an animal's vulnerability to predation (Petrovich et al., 2009; Kunwar et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Petrovich et al., 2009 and Kunwar et al., 2015, which describe the adaptive value of suppressing feeding during threat.

claim: The lateral septum shows increased c-fos expression under different stressful conditions.
source: Many brain regions are activated after stressful stimuli including the LS which shows increased c-fos expression under different stressful conditions (Sheehan et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sheehan et al., 2004, which describes c-fos expression in the LS after stress.

claim: LSNts neurons are specifically activated by active escape in response to stress.
source: We further showed that these neurons are specifically activated by active escape in response to stress and that chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons can suppress food intake and body weight via a projection to the LH.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing LSNts activation during active coping behaviors but not passive coping behaviors.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons can suppress food intake and body weight via a projection to the lateral hypothalamus.
source: We further showed that these neurons are specifically activated by active escape in response to stress and that chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons can suppress food intake and body weight via a projection to the LH.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons and optogenetic activation of LSNts terminals in the LH both reduce food intake.

claim: LSNts neurons respond to stress and specifically regulate feeding, but not other components of the stress response.
source: These neurons respond to stress and specifically regulate feeding, but not other components of the stress response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing LSNts effects on feeding but not on anxiety-related behaviors.

claim: LSNts neurons are selectively tuned to active escape and act to suppress food intake in mice.
source: These data thus delineate a molecularly defined limbic circuit selectively tuned to active escape and that acts to suppress food intake in mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing selective LSNts activation during active escape and effects on food intake.

claim: The lateral septum plays a role in mediating elements of a stress response.
source: These data are consistent with a number of prior studies suggesting that the LS plays a role in mediating elements of a stress response (Singewald et al., 2011; Bondi et al., 2007) though the cell types in the LS that mediate this response had not been identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Singewald et al., 2011 and Bondi et al., 2007, which describe the role of the LS in stress responses.

claim: The cell types in the lateral septum that mediate stress response had not been identified prior to this study.
source: These data are consistent with a number of prior studies suggesting that the LS plays a role in mediating elements of a stress response (Singewald et al., 2011; Bondi et al., 2007) though the cell types in the LS that mediate this response had not been identified.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Different neural populations within the lateral septum may be specially tuned to different aspects of the stress response.
source: This suggested that different neural populations within the LS may be specially tuned to different aspects of the stress response (sensory, movement, among others).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that LSNts neurons respond selectively to active coping, suggesting other populations may respond to other aspects.

claim: LSNts neurons do not regulate anxiety-like behaviors but instead reduce food intake.
source: We also found that LSNts neurons, in particular, do not regulate anxiety-like behaviors but instead reduce food intake suggesting that they link specific stressful stimuli to reduced food intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no effects on anxiety behaviors but significant effects on food intake.

claim: LSNts neuronal activation is tuned to active coping mechanisms that dispense with voluntary food intake until appropriate countermeasures to mitigate the stressful event have been enacted.
source: Thus, LSNts neuronal activation appears to be tuned to active coping mechanisms that dispense with voluntary food intake until appropriate countermeasures to mitigate the stressful event have been enacted.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing LSNts activation during active coping and effects on food intake suppression.

claim: The LSNts circuit would be useful for suppressing the urge to forage when predators are in the vicinity, thus serving an important evolutionary function.
source: For example, this circuit would be useful for suppressing the urge to forage when predators are in the vicinity, thus serving an important evolutionary function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an evolutionary function based on the observed circuit properties.

claim: Activation of LSNts neurons suppresses food intake even in animals that have been deprived of food.
source: Consistent with this, activation of LSNts neurons suppresses food intake even in animals that have been deprived of food, although future studies are needed to confirm the sufficiency of these neurons for stress-induced reductions in feeding by inhibiting the LSNts neurons during the stressful stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that chemogenetic activation of LSNts neurons suppresses food intake in fasted mice.

claim: Several stress paradigms used during in vivo calcium recordings were performed acutely which was insufficient to elicit a significant impact on food intake.
source: Many of the stress paradigms used during in vivo calcium recordings were performed acutely which we found to be insufficient to elicit a significant impact on food intake.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Several stressors such as foot shock can reduce food intake if applied chronically.
source: However, several of the stressors that were used, such as foot shock, can reduce food intake if applied chronically (Halataei et al., 2011; Rostamkhani et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Halataei et al., 2011 and Rostamkhani et al., 2016, which describe the effects of chronic stress on food intake.

claim: Neural plasticity and/or genetic alterations within the LSNts circuit could contribute to persistent maladaptive eating strategies.
source: If LSNts sufficiency is confirmed, neural plasticity and/or genetic alterations within this circuit (e.g. by mutations in the Nts gene as observed in Lutter et al., 2017 or changes in 'allostatic load'; McEwen and Akil, 2020) could contribute to persistent maladaptive eating strategies, such as those observed in eating disorders or in other cases obesity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential role for LSNts circuit alterations in eating disorders, supported by citations to Lutter et al., 2017 and McEwen and Akil, 2020.

claim: Other neural circuits mediate the effects of stressful stimuli that lead to freezing.
source: Presumably, other neural circuits mediate the effects of stressful stimuli that lead to freezing, raising the possibility that different circuits have evolved to process different types of stress, and that different types of chronic stress might be associated with different disorders.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that LSNts neurons do not respond to freezing, suggesting other circuits must mediate this response.

claim: Different circuits have evolved to process different types of stress.
source: Presumably, other neural circuits mediate the effects of stressful stimuli that lead to freezing, raising the possibility that different circuits have evolved to process different types of stress, and that different types of chronic stress might be associated with different disorders.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an evolutionary hypothesis based on the observed circuit specificity.

claim: Different types of chronic stress might be associated with different disorders.
source: Presumably, other neural circuits mediate the effects of stressful stimuli that lead to freezing, raising the possibility that different circuits have evolved to process different types of stress, and that different types of chronic stress might be associated with different disorders.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis about the relationship between stress types and disorders.

claim: The lateral septum neuronal population is mainly composed of GABAergic neurons although there are also some glutamatergic neurons.
source: The LS neuronal population is mainly composed of GABAergic neurons although there are also some glutamatergic neurons (Sunkin, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sunkin, 2013, which describes the neuronal composition of the LS.

claim: The LSNts neuronal population is heterogeneous and co-expresses a variety of molecules, including Glp1r.
source: In this study, we also explored the molecular diversity of LSNts neurons. Our findings suggest that the LSNts neuronal population is heterogeneous and co-express a variety of molecules, including Glp1r.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from viral-TRAP and in situ hybridization showing co-expression of multiple markers.

claim: Infusion of a Glp1r antagonist (Ex9) directly into the lateral septum diminished the anorexigenic effects of stress.
source: Consistent with our results, a previous report showed that the infusion of a Glp1r antagonist (Ex9) directly into the LS diminished the anorexigenic effects of stress, suggesting that Glp-1 signaling in LS contributes to this response (Terrill et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Terrill et al., 2018, which describes the effects of Glp1r antagonist on stress-induced anorexia.

claim: Glp-1 signaling in the lateral septum contributes to stress-induced anorexia.
source: Consistent with our results, a previous report showed that the infusion of a Glp1r antagonist (Ex9) directly into the LS diminished the anorexigenic effects of stress, suggesting that Glp-1 signaling in LS contributes to this response (Terrill et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the citation to Terrill et al., 2018, which showed that blocking Glp1r signaling reduces stress-induced anorexia.

claim: The lateral septum is innervated by pre-proglucagon (PPG) neurons in the brainstem expressing Glp-1.
source: The LS is innervated by pre-proglucagon (PPG) neurons in the brainstem expressing Glp-1 (Trapp and Cork, 2015) and these neurons have also been shown to mediate stress-induced hypophagia (Holt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Trapp and Cork, 2015, which describes the innervation of the LS by PPG neurons.

claim: Pre-proglucagon neurons in the brainstem expressing Glp-1 have been shown to mediate stress-induced hypophagia.
source: The LS is innervated by pre-proglucagon (PPG) neurons in the brainstem expressing Glp-1 (Trapp and Cork, 2015) and these neurons have also been shown to mediate stress-induced hypophagia (Holt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Holt et al., 2019, which describes the role of PPG neurons in stress-induced hypophagia.

claim: LSNts neurons that co-express Glp1r provide a link between brainstem circuits conveying stress to key output pathways to regulate feeding.
source: In aggregate, these data suggest that LSNts neurons that co-express Glp1r provide a link between brainstem circuits conveying stress to key output pathways to regulate feeding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that LSNts neurons co-express Glp1r, are activated by stress, and project to the LH to regulate feeding.

claim: The lateral septum receives inputs from many cortical and limbic areas, including the hippocampus.
source: The LS also receives inputs from many cortical and limbic areas, including the hippocampus (Tingley and Buzsáki, 2018; Azevedo et al., 2019; Jakab and Leranth, 1990) and in turn sends projections to many other brains areas (Deng et al., 2019) including the hypothalamus, hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, thalamus, and amygdala.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tingley and Buzsáki, 2018; Azevedo et al., 2019; and Jakab and Leranth, 1990, which describe the inputs to the LS.

claim: The lateral septum sends projections to many brain areas including the hypothalamus, hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, thalamus, and amygdala.
source: The LS also receives inputs from many cortical and limbic areas, including the hippocampus (Tingley and Buzsáki, 2018; Azevedo et al., 2019; Jakab and Leranth, 1990) and in turn sends projections to many other brains areas (Deng et al., 2019) including the hypothalamus, hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, thalamus, and amygdala.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Deng et al., 2019, which describes the projections from the LS.

claim: LSNts neurons play an important integratory function linking stress to food suppression and serving as an important integrator between the limbic system and the hypothalamus.
source: In summary, these data show that LSNts neurons play an important integratory function linking stress to food suppression and serving as an important integrator between the limbic system and the hypothalamus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing LSNts activation by stress, effects on food intake, and projections to the hypothalamus.

claim: The identification of LSNts neurons provides an entry point for understanding how complex inputs compete to generate an appropriate and adaptive response.
source: The identification of these neurons thus provides an entry point for understanding how complex inputs —in this case food deprivation versus danger—compete to generate an appropriate and adaptive response.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing the significance of the findings for future research.

claim: These findings may illuminate why in some cases stress can elicit a pathologic response such as in the case of eating disorders.
source: In addition, these findings may in time illuminate why in some cases stress can elicit a pathologic response such as in the case of eating disorders.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Higher-order, limbic brain regions integrate diverse sensory information to modulate subcortical feeding circuits in health and possibly disease.
source: These and other data further suggest that higher-order, limbic brain regions integrate diverse sensory information to modulate subcortical feeding circuits in health and possibly disease (Azevedo et al., 2019; Newmyer et al., 2019; Land et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Azevedo et al., 2019; Newmyer et al., 2019; and Land et al., 2014, which describe the role of limbic regions in modulating feeding circuits.
